steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Ways a game is drawn. This part covers Use it or avoid it. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

The draw rules are tools. [H] A rule of thumb, not a law: the side that is **worse** asks 'can I make a position come back?', and the side that is **better** asks 'which different move improves my position?'. A side with a winning plan usually changes the plan; a side with no way to make progress may be happy to repeat. Watch a side that is behind use it.

steps.title: Can the checks go on forever?

steps.caption: A lighter version first. Black's own pawns on g7 and h6 take squares from its king, so a single check leaves one square.

line.say: Check along the last row. The queen also covers g8, so only h7 is left.

claims.statement: After the queen checks, g8 is covered.
The queen can go to e8.

steps.caption: White is behind: three rooks against one queen. But the queen can check again and again. Checks that never end are called **perpetual check**.

line.say: Check along the last row. The queen also covers g8, so the king has one square: h7.
Check again, along the diagonal. The king must move or block.
Black goes back to h8. The starting position has returned.
The third appearance. White may claim a draw.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position as level, depth 16.
After Qe8 the queen attacks g8, so Black's king has only h7.
The queen can go to e8.

steps.caption: From the same start Black can also block with a pawn. The queen still has a new check each time.

line.say: A new check along the seventh row.
Check again. In each line the queen finds a check [engine, depth 16].

claims.statement: The engine rates the starting position as level, depth 16.
After the block the queen checks on the seventh row.
The queen can go to e8.

steps.text: In these examples every reply Black has allows another check; the bishop on g8 took the checks away. [I] My reading, not a published rule. Perpetual check is not a separate rule: the draw comes from the repetition rule, or from a claim when the same position keeps returning.

steps.caption: Now the other side. White is the one ahead and wants to win. Repeating would allow a draw claim, so White changes the plan.

line.say: The rook takes the seventh row. Black's king is cut off from everything below it.
Black's king can only shuffle on the last row.
The white king starts walking up to help. Every move now creates a new position.
Nothing repeats. The king is on its way to help the rook finish the game.

claims.statement: White to move wins in this position (tablebase).
The rook can go to a7.
The white king can step to f2.

steps.text: Five ways to a draw, in one place. **Stalemate** and **too few pieces left to give mate**: the game ends by itself. **Agreement:** both players say yes. **Repetition** and the **fifty-move rule:** a player must claim. The next lesson on draws covers positions with too few pieces.

steps.caption: The first draw on the list needs no claim at all.

line.say: The queen takes the last escape square. Black is not in check and has no move: stalemate, and the game is over.

claims.statement: After Qc7 the black king has no legal move.
After Qc7 nothing attacks the black king.

steps.caption: The same position, a different queen move. When you are winning, check before every move that the other king still has a move or is in check.

line.say: The queen checks along the last row and the king has nowhere to go: checkmate, not stalemate.

claims.statement: The queen can go to c8.

steps.text: **[H] A guess about why these rules exist.** Without a repetition rule, a worse side could shuffle for ever. Without a fifty-move rule, a side that cannot make progress could do the same. [I] Both rules seem to answer one question: how long may a game go on while nothing changes? Do you think they protect the stronger side or the weaker one? There is no checked answer.
